title: The Paper Bridge Test
learning_objectives: Use evidence from the story to explain a choice.
parent_prompts: Before reading: What do you notice in the title?
After reading: What helped the characters decide?

pages.text: Rae and Jo needed a paper bridge to carry a small wooden block across a gap between two desks. Their first flat sheet sagged before the block reached the middle.
pages.audio_script: Rae and Jo needed a paper bridge to carry a small wooden block across a gap between two desks. Their first flat sheet sagged before the block reached the middle.
pages.image_alt: A flat paper bridge sags between two desks under a wooden block.

pages.text: Jo suggested adding more paper, but Rae wanted to learn why the sheet bent. They marked the gap, used the same block, and agreed to change only one part at a time.
pages.audio_script: Jo suggested adding more paper, but Rae wanted to learn why the sheet bent. They marked the gap, used the same block, and agreed to change only one part at a time.
pages.image_alt: Rae and Jo plan a fair bridge test with the same block and a notebook.

pages.text: First, they folded the sheet into a shallow arch. The block stayed up for a moment, then slid toward the edge. A stronger shape was not enough without a steady place to rest.
pages.audio_script: First, they folded the sheet into a shallow arch. The block stayed up for a moment, then slid toward the edge. A stronger shape was not enough without a steady place to rest.
pages.image_alt: A paper arch holds a block briefly but slides near the desk edge.

pages.text: They folded two narrow rails and placed them along the desk edges. The arch no longer slipped, but its middle still dipped when the block was set down.
pages.audio_script: They folded two narrow rails and placed them along the desk edges. The arch no longer slipped, but its middle still dipped when the block was set down.
pages.image_alt: Paper rails hold the arch on the desk edges, though the middle bends.

pages.text: Rae noticed that a sheet folded like an accordion felt stiffer in her hands. They made a new bridge with repeated folds and kept the rails in place.
pages.audio_script: Rae noticed that a sheet folded like an accordion felt stiffer in her hands. They made a new bridge with repeated folds and kept the rails in place.
pages.image_alt: Rae folds a new paper bridge into accordion pleats.

pages.text: The block crossed the gap without touching the floor. Jo tested the same bridge twice more, moving the block slowly each time, while Rae watched the folds.
pages.audio_script: The block crossed the gap without touching the floor. Jo tested the same bridge twice more, moving the block slowly each time, while Rae watched the folds.
pages.image_alt: A wooden block crosses the folded paper bridge between desks.

pages.text: Their notes showed which change solved each problem: rails stopped slipping, and folds reduced bending. Neither child claimed the first idea was useless; it had shown them what to test.
pages.audio_script: Their notes showed which change solved each problem: rails stopped slipping, and folds reduced bending. Neither child claimed the first idea was useless; it had shown them what to test.
pages.image_alt: Rae and Jo compare their test notes with the rails and folded bridge.

pages.text: At the class display, Rae and Jo invited friends to predict which paper shape would carry the block. They explained that a useful design grows from careful tests, not from guessing once.
pages.audio_script: At the class display, Rae and Jo invited friends to predict which paper shape would carry the block. They explained that a useful design grows from careful tests, not from guessing once.
pages.image_alt: Rae and Jo show classmates their tested paper bridge.

quiz.prompt: Why do Rae and Jo change one part at a time?
quiz.explanation: Page 2 says they agree to change only one part at a time to understand the bending.
Page 7 states that rails stopped slipping.
